intro: The finale of Brahms’s Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98, marked Allegro energico e passionato, is a set of thirty variations on an eight-note theme and ends in E minor. At its centre, a solo flute and a trombone chorale slow the pace.

sections.label: Theme · Eight wind and brass chords
sections.mNote: A rising line with a chromatic A♯

sections.label: Var 1–11 · Plucked strings, then running notes
sections.mNote: The eight-bar pattern passes through strings and winds.

sections.label: Var 12–13 · Flute solo, then E major
sections.mNote: The bars double in length; oboe and clarinet follow the flute.

sections.label: Var 14–15 · Trombone chorale, E major
sections.mNote: The low brass play in E major.

sections.label: Var 16–24 · Opening chords over altered bass
sections.mNote: The return to three crotchet beats begins in A minor.

sections.label: Var 25–30 · C major, then descending thirds
sections.mNote: A passage in C major precedes the last variations in E minor

sections.label: Coda · Più allegro, cascading strings
sections.mNote: The eight-bar pattern changes at the Più allegro.

relations.label: The harmonic cycle returns
relations.basis: The passacaglia uses recurring eight-bar harmonic cycles. These neighbouring passages sit inside the opening variations, where the listening note near 140 s describes the retained cycle; the relation is harmonic, not a claim of an unchanged tune. CENS diagonal mean 0.918, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 18 s (cache/form/brahms-4-finale.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening theme, winds and brass
cues.text: Winds and brass play eight chords, and the strings rest. The upper line rises from E towards B, with A sharpened to A♯ on the way. These eight bars return thirty times, sometimes deep inside the orchestral texture.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 4, IV, bars 1–8, Simrock first edition (1886). Theme and thirty variations described by Kelly Dean Hansen: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Source of the theme in Bach
cues.text: The pattern comes from the closing chorus of Bach’s cantata Nach dir, Herr, verlanget mich, BWV 150. Brahms added a chromatic note, A♯, the fifth note of the theme, which leads up to B.
cues.evidence: Bach source and added chromatic note: Jan Swafford, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-4. Hansen identifies A♯ as the fifth note of the theme: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.

cues.title: Variation 12, solo flute
cues.text: The bars double in length, from 3/4 to 3/2. A solo flute plays a melody over the same eight-bar pattern, with short off-beat chords in the strings and horns.
cues.evidence: Variation 12, bars 97–104; the score retains the note-value speed while changing the metre. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trombone chorale in E major
cues.text: In E major, the trombones play a chorale with bassoons and horns. Violas and cellos follow with short rising arpeggios. Rests separate the phrases, and the cadences arrive late.
cues.evidence: Variations 14–15, bars 113–128; trombone chorale and delayed plagal cadences. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Elisabeth von Herzogenberg, 1885
cues.text: In August 1885 Brahms sent Elisabeth von Herzogenberg the first movement from Mürzzuschlag. He wrote that “Cherries never get ripe for eating in these parts” and asked her to say if she did not like the taste. He added: “I’m not at all eager to write a bad No. 4.”
cues.evidence: Brahms to Elisabeth von Herzogenberg, August 1885, quoted by Jan Swafford in his Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-4

cues.title: Return of the opening chords
cues.text: The opening chords return with force, and 3/2 contracts to 3/4. A minor now stands plainly at the beginning, with A in the bass. The strings follow the winds with a descending scale.
cues.evidence: Variation 16, bars 129–136; changed bass, restored 3/4 and descending string scale. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variations 26–28, C major
cues.text: The late variations move into C major. Winds play in thirds over pizzicato lower strings, and violas and violins pass triplet arpeggios between them. A bass rising by semitones leads back towards E minor.
cues.evidence: Variations 26–28, bars 209–232; C-major passage and chromatic bass leading back to E. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html. The section boundary covers the late variation group.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, Più allegro
cues.text: The coda (bars 253–260) is marked Più allegro. Winds and brass rise against descending runs in the strings, then hold the theme’s chromatic note, the former A♯, now spelt B♭. Timpani rolls and pauses prolong it.
cues.evidence: Coda, bars 253–260; the former A♯ is written B♭ and prolonged. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final cadences in E minor
cues.text: The closing cadences stay in E minor. Repeated three-note upbeats lead into the tonic chord, and the timpani roll under the final chords. The G♮ is kept, so the movement ends in the minor.
cues.evidence: Coda, bars 289–311; E-minor cadences and final timpani roll. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The chords separated across the beats
transitions.from: Theme · Eight wind and brass chords
transitions.to: Var 1–11 · Plucked strings, then running notes
transitions.how: The harmony is repeated, including the A♯ that moves towards B, but the orchestra divides its attacks. Horns and timpani play on the first beat and plucked strings on the second. The third beat is silent. For the first four bars the trombones join the plucked strings on the second beat.
transitions.evidence: Theme and variation 1, bars 1–16; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.

transitions.title: Change to 3/2 for flute solo
transitions.from: Var 1–11 · Plucked strings, then running notes
transitions.to: Var 12–13 · Flute solo, then E major
transitions.how: In variations 11–12 (bars 89–104), a late dominant chord on B prepares the return to E minor. The metre changes from 3/4 to 3/2 and the note values keep their speed. A solo flute plays the melody through the longer bars, accompanied by short off-beat chords in the horns and strings.

transitions.title: Oboe phrase into low brass chorale
transitions.from: Var 12–13 · Flute solo, then E major
transitions.how: A descending oboe phrase continues across the join and delays the cadence from A major to E major. Trombones, bassoons and horns take over with chorale phrases. Violas and cellos follow with upward arpeggios, and a horn line later links the two chorale variations.

transitions.title: Variation 15 to Variation 16
transitions.to: Var 16–24 · Opening chords over altered bass
transitions.how: In bars 121–136, across Variations 15 and 16, the flute’s descending link breaks off on A minor. After the pause, the winds play the opening chords again with A in the bass, and the broad 3/2 bars contract to 3/4. The strings enter with a forceful descending scale. No cadence in E major follows.

transitions.title: Final variation extended into the coda
transitions.from: Var 25–30 · C major, then descending thirds
transitions.how: Wide leaps in the strings and horns extend the final variation beyond eight bars. The timpani become more prominent, and an augmented chord leaves the harmony between E and C major. At Più allegro, winds and brass begin the rising theme over cascading strings. Its fifth note is respelt B♭, which delays the expected continuation.
transitions.evidence: Extension and coda, bars 249–260; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus98.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 4, Op. 98, full score (Berlin: N. Simrock, 1886, plate 8686; first edition)
source.locator: IV. Allegro energico e passionato, printed pp. 77–113; eight-bar theme, thirty variations and Più allegro coda.

timeline.note: Winds and brass play the eight chords; trumpet and timpani emphasise the fifth, with A♯.
Horns and timpani mark the first beat, plucked strings the second; trombones join the strings for four bars.
Soft winds, horns and timpani over low strings, rising to a marked forte.
Winds and brass join plucked upper strings; cellos and basses bow their arpeggios.
The first violins play the melody above off-beat inner strings; the bassoons double the theme in the bass.
Quicker wind and string figures; horns and trumpets hold chords.
Held horn and trumpet notes beneath soft strings and winds.
The solo flute plays the melody in 3/2 above off-beat chords in the violins, violas and horns.
Oboe and clarinet continue the slow variations, piano dolce.
E major: an oboe link, then trombones, bassoons and horns in chorale phrases.
The scoring of the chorale widens to winds, horns, trumpets and trombones, playing soft chords.
The winds and brass return with the opening chords, and the strings add a descending scale.
Full orchestra with timpani; the variations continue in fortissimo.
A brief passage of held wind and brass notes under pianissimo violin scales.
The tutti returns, fortissimo through the next variations.
Quiet wind thirds and plucked low strings give way to flowing string arpeggios.
Poco ritardando and crescendo. Trombones and timpani return.
Coda, Più allegro: winds and brass play the theme over string arpeggios.

composer.epithet: Composer who completed his First Symphony at the age of forty-three and began his Second beside an Austrian lake the following summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853 a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music to them. Robert Schumann heard in him a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen (New Paths). Publishers became interested. Brahms was now expected to fulfil a public prophecy before most of the public had heard any of his music. His piano sonatas were large-scale works. The symphonies Schumann expected took much longer to arrive.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob, earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. He studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
